title: Purposeful & Active “Reading to Learn”
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Prompted by a nursing professor who asked why college students cannot teach themselves from a textbook, Stuart answers that students get too few chances to learn from reading and are rarely taught how. His remedy has two stages. Quantity first: teachers tally how much reading every student is actually given, which sidesteps debate with hard data, and then increase it with efficient routines such as an article of the week. Quality next: teachers explicitly communicate the purpose of reading to learn and model it. An anecdote about a diligent student, Anna, who took notes whenever something felt worth writing down shows how reading as duty falls short of the stance of being a student of the text.
points: Students struggle to learn from reading because they have too few reading opportunities and too little instruction in how to read to learn.
Counting the reading every student receives across courses gives an undebatable baseline for increasing volume.
Quantity is treated as triage, since quality of practice matters little until enough practice is guaranteed.
Even motivated students may read out of duty, so teachers need to model active, self-regulated reading with a clear purpose.
quotes: So, again, my question is: Why aren’t college students able to learn from reading?” My answer — which is liable to be wrong, so take it for what it is — is twofold: first, they aren’t given enough opportunities to learn from reading; and second, they aren’t adequately taught how to learn from reading.

I find that this cuts past debates about how to fit more reading into the content areas because it starts with undebatable data: point blank, how much reading is already expected, for every child? Interestingly enough, this exercise is often enlightening for English Language Arts teachers, too.

To use a sports metaphor, all that we’re doing at this point is deciding how many reading practice sessions all of our kids are guaranteed to have. Until this happens, the quality of those practices is somewhat irrelevant.

The quantity exercises above are really triage work — these are the lowest hanging fruits for moving the needle on reading achievement; they establish conditions in which readers can grow. Once this triage work is done, it’s time to attend to the long-term quality of a school’s work around reading, and this is where the nine moves for teaching with texts come in.

This was an epiphany for me. Here I had a hard-working kid, a kid who does her reading consistently, a kid who fully wants to succeed and believes she can succeed and feels like she belongs (in short, she has the four academic mindsets), but she was still doing the reading primarily because it was something she had been told to do. For her, doing the reading was “learning as duty” — and while that is an important conception of learning, it’s not a good one when we’re helping kids learn to learn from reading.

Instead, the stance we want kids to take when approaching a reading to learn task is, “Okay, right now I am a student of this text, and my job is to learn as much as I can from it. I can ask questions of this teacher-text, but it’s only going to answer with itself. I can also ask questions of other sources — ‘Google, define bellicose’ — and I can ask my peers or Mr. Stuart tomorrow if I get stuck beyond that.
